blocks.text: Aromatic hydrocarbons that contain only one benzene ring in this structure are known as monocyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. We will look into nomenclature of monocyclic aromatic compounds first. There are two styles of naming benzene derivatives. One in which the compound is named with the suffix 'benzene' and one with no benzene (special name).
When a single substituent is present on a benzene, it is a monosubstituted benzene.

items: Most of the monosubstituted benzenes are named with the base name 'benzene' and using the substituent group as a prefix, such as chlorobenzene, nitrobenzene and methyl benzene.

Many monosubstituted benzenes have common names; some of these names have been included in IUPAC nomenclature as base names for the structure. e.g, phenol, toluene, aniline, etc. Common names in bold face given below are considered to be IUPAC correct base names for structures. The substituent in a monosubstituted benzene is always at C-1, so there is no need to number its location.
Some benzene derivatives have special names, which are accepted as IUPAC names, e.g., benzene carboxylic acid, benzene sulphonic acid, etc.

blocks.alt: Nine benzene rings, each with one substituent, named as in the book: toluene (methylbenzene), phenol (benzenol), anisole (methoxybenzene), aniline (benzenamine), benzaldehyde (benzenecarbaldehyde), benzoic acid (benzenecarboxylic acid), benzene sulphonic acid, nitrobenzene and chlorobenzene.
blocks.caption: Common names of monosubstituted benzenes (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 62-63).

blocks.text: Disubstituted benzenes are compounds when two substituents are present on the benzene ring. They are named according to the following rules.

items: The carbon to which a higher priority substituent is attached is C₁. Others are numbered accordingly. The order of priority of substituents (left to right) is: -COOH, -CN, -CHO, -COCH₃, -OH, -NH₂, -OR, -R
If both substituents are the same priority then the carbon having a substituent lower in alphabets is designated as C₁.

blocks.text: The following examples explain how the disubstituted benzenes are named.

blocks.alt: Three disubstituted benzenes with numbered ring carbons: 3-hydroxybenzoic acid (COOH on C-1, OH on C-3; acid is higher priority than alcohol), 4-isopropylphenol, also 4-(1-methylethyl)-phenol (OH on C-1, isopropyl on C-4; the phenol alcohol is C-1), and 1-bromo-2-chlorobenzene (Br on C-1, Cl on C-2; bromo is before chloro in the alphabet).
blocks.caption: Names of disubstituted benzenes (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 63).

blocks.title: Did You Know?
blocks.text: Disubstituted benzenes have common names with reference to the relationship between the two substituents. Instead of using numbers to indicate substituents on a benzene ring, ortho- (o-), meta- (m-), or para (p-) can be used in place of positional markers when there are two substituents on the benzene ring.

blocks.alt: Three dibromobenzenes with ring carbons numbered 1 to 6: Br on C-1 and C-2 labelled ortho (1,2), Br on C-1 and C-3 labelled meta (1,3), and Br on C-1 and C-4 labelled para (1,4).
blocks.caption: Ortho, meta and para positions of benzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 63).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed drawing labels 1,4-dibromobenzene 'ortho (1,3)'; bromine atoms at positions 1 and 4 are para (1,4), as drawn above.
Aromatic hydrocarbons that contain two or more benzene rings in their molecules are known as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.

blocks.alt: Kekule structures of naphthalene, two fused rings (C10H8); anthracene, three rings in a straight line (C14H10); and phenanthrene, three rings joined at an angle (C14H10).
blocks.caption: Three polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (original structures after the book's examples).
blocks.long_description: In polycyclic arenes neighbouring rings share a C-C edge. Anthracene and phenanthrene have the same formula, C14H10, but their rings are joined differently: in a line and at an angle.

blocks.alt: Six arenes numbered i to vi: (i) benzene with NO2 groups on C-1 and C-3; (ii) with Cl on two neighbouring carbons; (iii) with OH and Br opposite each other; (iv) with CH3, a Cl next to it and a Cl opposite it; (v) with CH3 and three NO2 groups at the two neighbouring carbons and the opposite carbon; (vi) benzene carrying C(=O)-O-CH3.
blocks.caption: The arenes of Quick Check 20.2 (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 64).
